## Supported distribution and parameterization

`update_priors(outcome = ...)` reconciles beliefs about a Gaussian conditional expected
response, not individual observations. The initial scope is identity-link
regression with an intercept, numeric predictors, and independent Normal
coefficient priors. Existing coefficient-only candidate selection runs first;
Student's t selections are rejected rather than approximated by Normals.
The residual-scale distribution is not optimized. Offsets are already
unsupported by `identify_priors()`.

The existing frozen model terms and prediction-matrix builder construct each
configuration's row. All original predictors must be supplied once in `at`;
transformations and interactions are evaluated using those terms. Columns
are aligned with the original coefficients. For slope columns, their original
model-matrix means are subtracted, matching rstanarm's centered intercept.
Independence is imposed in this centered parameterization, not in an
uncentered intercept parameterization. The latter generally has correlations.

For baseline means $\mu_{0j}$ and SDs $s_{0j}$, optimization uses dimensionless
variables $u_j$ and $\ell_j$:

$$
\mu_j=\mu_{0j}+s_{0j}u_j,\qquad s_j=s_{0j}\exp(\ell_j).
$$

At row $x_k$, $M_k\sim N(x_k^T\mu,\sum_j x_{kj}^2s_j^2)$.
Mean and mode constraints therefore use $x_k^T\mu$; inequality probabilities
use the corresponding Normal CDF (or its upper tail). A finite Normal has
probabilities strictly between zero and one at finite thresholds. A recorded
boundary target is evaluated against its declared positive acceptance band;
it is not claimed to be attained exactly. An interior point of that band may
initialize the search without changing the recorded answer. No residual noise
is added to these calculations.

## Compatibility before reconciliation

A failure of local optimization is not an impossibility certificate. The
pre-check uses the actual centered rows $x_i$ and keeps every stated answer.
It reports the configurations and within-configuration belief numbers involved;
the reported set need not be a minimal conflicting subset.

For $M_i\sim N(m_i,s_i^2)$, a location belief gives an interval for $m_i$.
A lower-tail probability acceptance interval $[p_L,p_U]$ gives

$$
h-\Phi^{-1}(p_U)s_i\le m_i\le h-\Phi^{-1}(p_L)s_i.
$$

Upper-tail statements give the corresponding reversed bounds without
subtracting a tiny tail probability from 1. Infinite quantile endpoints simply
remove a side of the inequality. Intersecting these linear half-spaces in
$(m_i,s_i)$ and eliminating $m_i$ yields necessary lower and upper SD bounds.
Statements at identical centered rows are combined, even if entered through
separate calls. These bounds use the **acceptance intervals**, not just exact
point targets, and are rounded outward to avoid overstating incompatibility.

Let $A_{ij}=x_{ij}^2$ and $v_j=\sigma_j^2$. Independent coefficient priors require

$$
Av\in[L,U],\qquad v\ge0,
$$

where $L,U$ are the implied variance bounds. Allowing zero variances here
makes an outer feasibility set: an empty set also rules out strictly positive
variances. The diagnostic does not declare a zero-only feasible boundary to
be a valid independent-Normal prior.

One certificate compares any two rows. If $A_{ij}\le cA_{kj}$ for every column,
then $Var(M_i)\le c Var(M_k)$ for all nonnegative variances. A column with zero
denominator and positive numerator makes this bound unavailable; it is not
silently ignored. This handles arbitrary centered configurations, not only
houses differing in one predictor.

For the interview example with area centered at 2,014.94, houses of 1,500 and
3,000 square feet have area coordinates -514.94 and 985.06. At common age and
bedroom settings, other variance contributions have ratio 1. Therefore their
SD ratio is at most $985.06/514.94\approx1.913$. Most likely prices of 300,000
and 500,000 with 5% below 250,000 and 400,000 imply exact SDs
$50000/|\Phi^{-1}(.05)|$ and $100000/|\Phi^{-1}(.05)|$: ratio 2. The actual
check uses the SD ranges implied by the supplied tolerances, which still
exclude 1.913 under the default strict matching rule. Wider **explicit**
acceptance intervals can describe a different, compatible problem; they do
not make the original point targets compatible.

Pairwise ratios are not sufficient with many configurations. A convex
squared-distance search looks for a separating vector $r$ satisfying

$$
A^T r\ge0,\qquad \sup_{y\in[L,U]}r^Ty<0.
$$

These inequalities independently contradict $Av\in[L,U]$ for every $v\ge0$.
The search's convergence flag is never used as an impossibility proof. The
witness inequalities and a separation margin are checked separately, after
unit-invariant positive row/column scaling. Roundoff corrections are supported
only on finite upper bounds; no infinite bound is replaced by a finite cap.
For example, variances at centered coordinates -1, 0 and 2 must satisfy
$V(2)=4V(-1)-3V(0)$ in an intercept-plus-slope model. Requested variances
2, 1 and 3 violate this relation, even though pairwise ratio checks pass.

Probability-consistency and location acceptance-interval checks remain.
Nearly singular mean systems are not declared impossible by truncating small
singular directions; their numerical resolution may instead remain unresolved.
These are **necessary-condition diagnostics**, not a complete decision procedure
for coupled means and variances: probability bands can couple $m_i$ and $s_i$
more tightly than their separate bounds. Passing the checks does not prove
compatibility. If no certificate is found and no feasible prior is verified,
status is numerically unresolved, not mathematically incompatible. Solver or
initialization errors retain the answers and block simulation, export and fit.
Extremely narrow or ill-conditioned cases may remain unresolved.

## Numerical matching versus interview precision

The default absolute `belief()` tolerance remains `1e-6` for backward
compatibility. It is not a model of how accurately an expert reports an answer.
No default is silently expanded using the response magnitude or backend prior.
For an expected-price mode reported to the nearest 10,000 units,
`belief(mode=300000, tolerance=5000)` explicitly allows the model's mode to
fall within that reporting interval. A probability reported to the nearest
percentage point can use `tolerance=.005`. These tolerances describe matching
precision, while the probability targets describe prior uncertainty. Establish
them during elicitation, not after inspecting whether the model fits.

Location tolerances have response units and must transform with those units;
probability tolerances are unchanged by unit conversions. Optimizer convergence
and certificate-roundoff thresholds are separate dimensionless quantities and
do not widen the declared belief intervals. Strict constraints remain available
through smaller explicit positive tolerances.

A future context-scaled default (for example, a specified fraction of a fixed
response SD) could preserve affine unit invariance, but would require a stated
elicitation-precision policy. A percentage of the target alone changes meaning
under response translations and near zero. Neither policy is introduced here;
interview precision is left explicit for separate evaluation.

## Three priorities, without preference weights

1. All outcome beliefs must hold within their absolute `belief()` tolerances.
2. Among feasible priors, minimize the maximum **dimensionless** excess
   violation of explicit coefficient beliefs. Acceptance tolerances determine
   whether a statement holds; they are not preference weights. The former
   objective, $\max_i\max(0, |a_i-t_i|/\tau_i-1)$, made the common default
   absolute tolerance impose different preferences when units changed.
3. Among those solutions, minimize

$$
\mathrm{KL}(Q\,||\,P_0)=\frac12\sum_j
\left[u_j^2+\exp(2\ell_j)-1-2\ell_j\right].
$$

Here $Q$ is the adjusted joint Normal prior and $P_0$ the original
coefficient-only selection. This direction penalizes departures in means
and scales relative to the baseline. Explicit beliefs enter priority 2;
backend defaults enter only priority 3. No arbitrary weighting of explicit
beliefs against defaults is used. A parameter with zero contribution at all
specified configurations stays at its baseline unless another explicit
constraint requires otherwise.

### Comparing compromises

For a mean, mode or SD belief about coefficient $j$, define

$$
d_i = (a_i-t_i)/s_{0j},\qquad
L_i=-\tau_i/s_{0j},\quad U_i=\tau_i/s_{0j}.
$$

The discrepancy and its tolerance band are measured using baseline coefficient
uncertainty, rather than dollars, dollars per square foot, or tolerance counts.
SD discrepancies are scaled as positive quantities, without a location shift.

For a probability statement $P(\beta_j<h)=p_i$, let
$q_i=(h-\mu_j)/s_j$ and $z_i=\Phi^{-1}(p_i)$. For an upper-tail statement use
$q_i=(\mu_j-h)/s_j$. In both cases the achieved probability is $\Phi(q_i)$.
Define

$$
d_i=q_i-z_i,\quad
L_i=\Phi^{-1}(\max(0,p_i-\tau_i))-z_i,\quad
U_i=\Phi^{-1}(\min(1,p_i+\tau_i))-z_i.
$$

This compares the threshold's achieved and requested positions in a standard
Normal distribution. It respects the meaning of small tail probabilities,
rather than equating a fixed probability-point error in every part of the CDF.
The calculation uses $q_i$ directly; it does not invert a rounded CDF value.
An endpoint of 0 or 1 removes that side of the constraint through an infinite
probit bound, without clipping achieved values or replacing the probability target.

For either kind of belief, priority 2 minimizes

$$
T=\max_i v_i,\qquad v_i=\max(0,L_i-d_i,d_i-U_i).
$$

Thus a belief within its original acceptance band has zero excess sacrifice.
This is an explicitly chosen Normal-coordinate metric, not a universal distance
between all possible kinds of beliefs. It supplies a common, dimensionless
comparison without coefficient-specific preference weights. Means and spreads
remain free to change together. Raw discrepancies, absolute tolerances and
satisfaction flags are retained separately; the comparison metric never relabels
a relaxed belief as satisfied. Standardized coefficient beliefs display raw
quantities in their entered units, while optimization uses their equivalent
original-scale constraints.

### Scope of unit invariance

For simple predictors, $x'_j=a_jx_j+b_j$ with $a_j>0$ implies
$\beta'_j=\beta_j/a_j$. Since
$x'_j-\bar x'_j=a_j(x_j-\bar x_j)$, the centered intercept and independence
are preserved. Baseline and adjusted slope SDs transform by $1/a_j$ as well.
The optimization variables, dimensionless sacrifice and KL divergence are
unchanged. Positive affine response changes also preserve this structure when
intercept locations and outcome statements receive the corresponding shift.

Equivalent specifications must transform *absolute location/SD tolerances*,
not just targets and probability thresholds. Probability tolerances are unchanged.
The default `1e-6` remains an absolute numerical acceptance tolerance for backward
compatibility. Leaving it unchanged after rescaling describes slightly different
acceptance bands; very small differences may therefore remain. It no longer
assigns arbitrary cross-coefficient importance to those units.

The claim covers rescalings of centered model-matrix columns that preserve the
supported independent-Normal joint prior. General changes of centering, rotations,
or affine transformations inside polynomial/interaction formulas can mix
coefficients and induce covariance. Such changes need correlated priors to be
equivalent; unrestricted parameterization invariance is not claimed. Extreme
scales whose tolerances cannot be represented reliably may remain unresolved.

Adding another outcome specification recomputes from the same coefficient-only
baseline. Updating coefficient beliefs rebuilds that baseline and reconciles
all retained outcomes. Neither addition mutates its input. Original statements,
entered standardized units, IDs, defaults, and candidate diagnostics are
retained; achieved joint diagnostics are stored separately.

## Analytical benchmark

With fixed variances and one exact location constraint, minimizing KL over
means is minimum Mahalanobis displacement:

$$
\mu_{new}=\mu_0+
\frac{\Sigma_0 x}{x^T\Sigma_0x}(m-x^T\mu_0).
$$

This is used to initialize the numerical search and as an independent
regression-test benchmark. The numerical solution with a nonzero acceptance
tolerance may lie slightly inside its tolerance boundary. The formula does
not solve the general problem with changing variances, multiple probability
constraints, or prioritized coefficient beliefs.

## Numerical search and reliability

The implementation uses deterministic augmented-Lagrangian optimization,
BFGS, analytic gradients, and a log-SD parameterization. A dimensionless
maximum-violation variable implements priority 2. Constraints are scaled by
baseline SDs (probabilities use unit scale); this is numerical conditioning,
not a preference weight. Coefficient constraints use the dimensionless bands
above. A nonzero priority-2 optimum is retained to relative accuracy `1e-6`
before KL minimization (zero remains zero). This small numerical allowance
opens a nearly optimal face for the KL search; it is not a statistical weight.
The final score is checked against this bound, and KL must not materially exceed
its value at the priority-2 solution. A small interior tolerance margin
reduces rounding problems; an outcome-feasibility retry removes that margin
when tolerance intervals have a narrow intersection. A final Jacobian-based
correction restores numerical feasibility. Outcome feasibility is checked in
actual belief units; roundoff-size coefficient-bound errors (up to `1e-10` in
comparison units) cannot repeatedly undo that correction. A zero-sacrifice result
must still satisfy every raw coefficient tolerance. Conflict certificates are
also evaluated in dimensionless coordinates. Actual, unscaled belief residuals
are always recomputed before accepting a result.

A failed KL stage with a nonzero compromise bound can now be refined by a
feasible Newton log-barrier search. It first sharpens the minimax epigraph
solution, then minimizes KL on the **same relative near-minimax face**. This is an equivalent numerical formulation,
not a change to the priorities or acceptance bands. At the fixed compromise bound,
a coefficient probability band becomes a pair of linear inequalities in its mean
and SD, using Normal quantiles. Outcome probability bands become inequalities
in the outcome mean and the norm of its coefficient SD contributions. Means stay
in baseline-SD units; positive SDs use the pre-polishing priority-2 coordinate
scales. Keeping those scales avoids a nearly vanishing minimax SD becoming a
poor KL coordinate scale; it imposes no bound on selected SDs.
Analytic gradients and Hessians, diagonal preconditioning, and a slack-variable
interior search avoid the ill-conditioning of very large penalty parameters on
thin faces. When possible, Newton steps use a QR least-squares solve instead of
forming normal equations, which would square the conditioning problem.
Minimax polishing is important here: even a small stopping error can materially
change the variance budget on a thin face and make results depend on units. This recovery path uses base R and adds no dependency.

The resulting point is converted back to the original log-SD coordinates. It must
pass the **unchanged** original outcome, minimax-bound, KL-ordering, feasibility,
and nonnegative-multiplier stationarity checks. Solver stopping codes alone are
not sufficient. A failed recovery remains numerically unresolved. In particular,
this does not claim an exact attained minimax optimum when an unconstrained
coefficient SD approaches zero: the existing relative `1e-6` near-minimax face
remains the numerical convention, and positive SDs are still required.

When a solve fails, technical summaries distinguish original coefficient priors,
unverified attempted priors and their belief evaluations, and retained fallback
priors. Attempted quantities are not labeled as selected distributions. Successful
summaries identify the verified reconciled priors instead. Ordinary summaries
continue to omit optimization details.

The routine consumes no random numbers. It is a deterministic local search,
not a proof of a global optimum or uniqueness. A single outcome belief cannot
identify every coefficient mean and variance. The minimax/KL criterion chooses
an anchored solution to underdetermined specifications. Diagnostics include
targets, achieved quantities, raw discrepancies, numerical tolerances,
residuals in tolerance units, dimensionless discrepancies and excess violations,
optimizer codes, iteration counts, scaled constraint violations, objective values, and local
stationarity residuals. A nonnegative multiplier certificate checks first-order
optimality; a feasible result without a sufficiently small certificate residual
is not accepted. This local check does not certify a global optimum.

Some conflicts have direct certificates: incompatible location constraints
against the design matrix, or impossible ordered CDF requirements at the same
configuration. These are labeled incompatible. Other failures are labeled
numerically unresolved rather than claiming a proof of mathematical
impossibility. In either case, predictive checking, export, and fitting stop.
Compatible beliefs satisfy all explicit and outcome statements; reconciled
beliefs satisfy the outcomes but warn about the original coefficient statements
that were relaxed. They are never relabeled as satisfied.

Extremely ill-conditioned designs or demanding probability constraints may
remain unresolved. More general response families, categorical predictors,
correlated priors, or unsupported distribution shapes require future methods;
no silent approximation is attempted.

## Checking and backend fidelity

`summary(priors)` reports each configuration, requested and achieved outcome
beliefs and one grouped table of changed coefficient priors and compromised
original beliefs. Before shows the original prior or requested belief value;
After shows the adjusted prior or achieved value. The table uses `N(mean,SD)`,
omits unchanged priors and satisfied beliefs, and contains no optimization
statistics. Unverified results are flagged rather than presented as selected.
`summary(priors, diagnostics=TRUE)` retains the complete before/after comparison
and adds raw and normalized discrepancies, numerical tolerances, KL divergence,
convergence and stationarity details.
`check_prior()` samples the adjusted coefficients using the unchanged prior
predictive machinery; `expected` excludes residual noise and `simulated`
includes it. `as_rstanarm()` exports adjusted Normal locations and scales with
`autoscale=FALSE`, retaining the centered intercept and unchanged residual prior.
`fit()` uses that same export. Changed data, selected distributions, or stale
reconciliation diagnostics are rejected. Export remains restricted to the
existing verified rstanarm version; automated tests do not require Stan sampling.

The brms adapter uses the same proper, rstanarm-derived reference priors and
the same centered model matrix. Gaussian reconciliation therefore gives the
same selected distributions for equivalent models. `as_brms()` exports the
reconciled Normal coefficients individually and the centered intercept with
`class = "Intercept"`; it overrides native brms defaults. Sigma is unchanged.
Random effects and distributional regression remain outside this workflow.
